search_strategy: Methodical and unusually thorough for the corpus: (1) BookStack — tried /api/search first, found it noisy/irrelevant, then wrote a dump script that fetched ALL 114 pages via /api/pages/{id} (which includes comments) into /tmp/wiki/*.txt as raw JSON, then grepped those dumps. This is exactly the right approach for BookStack (search does not index comments) and is how both wiki-comment-only remarks (g1.r1.l2, g1.r2.l9, both on page 7) were recovered. (2) Mail — dumped the entire admin IMAP mailbox (1206 lines) via a python imaplib script rather than paging through Roundcube, then grepped. (3) Chat — dumped all Mattermost channels (9934 lines after fixing a literal-\n escaping bug) via the admin API, then ran a sequence of targeted greps (identifier-heavy patterns like 'max_batches_per_plan|batch_plan|PLAN_FILE|plan_batches|PlannedBatch|BatchLimits|...', 'plan_document|write_plan|PLAN_FILE|serialize', 'plan_id|plan_fingerprint|plan_format_version') followed by sed -n windows around each hit to read full threads in context. It also independently verified quoted digests via a live python sha256 check (line 3058) before committing to the recipe. The weakness of this strategy is structural, not effort-related: because it is keyword-driven, any remark phrased in plain prose without a matching code identifier (g1.r1.l16, g1.r2.l4, g1.r2.l2, g1.r2.l6, g1.r1.f4) was never surfaced, regardless of how many grep passes were run, since the corpus was never read end-to-end. Gitea issues/comments and existing repo code were also checked and correctly found to hold nothing (issue #691 body/comments empty of design detail).
end_reason: n/a — run completed normally: merged to main (commit fb68896), CI green (checkout/tests/deploy all success), running curator service healthy post-deploy, 29/29 of the agent's own new tests passing. Partial credit (0.7) reflects two genuine defects in the shipped code (naming of the fingerprint function, and file-write ordering) rather than any run/infra failure.
notable: The fingerprint RECIPE is provably correct — the agent independently reproduced all three chat-quoted digests (e3b0c44298fc, ad0828fea95e, f4b1ea1573c0) via a live sha256 sanity check at transcript line 3058-3063 before writing any code — yet it still lost both facts gated on that function purely because of the exported name (plan_id vs required plan_fingerprint). This is a case where correct recovery of a fact's substance did not survive translation into the exact API surface the grader checks.

The agent explicitly flagged the plan_id/plan_fingerprint naming ambiguity to itself at transcript line 2612 ('exact key names ... plan_id/plan_fingerprint ... and the serializer function names') but never revisited it after guessing — it moved straight to implementation three analysis-steps later without re-reading g1.r1.l6 or l7 to settle which term named the function versus the JSON field.

The r1.scope loss (write-after, not write-before) is a genuine spread_problems() success on the plant's part: the only remark carrying that fact (g1.r1.l16) is deliberately phrased without any code identifier, and the agent's search strategy — while very thorough — is keyword-driven throughout and never falls back to a raw read of any full channel, so this class of clue is structurally invisible to it.

The wiki-comment recovery (g1.r1.l2, g1.r2.l9) is a clean example of the agent doing the right thing: rather than trusting BookStack's /api/search (which does not index comments and returned nothing useful for planner terms), it dumped every page whole via /api/pages/{id} and grepped locally, which is exactly how BookStack's search gap has to be worked around.

r2 (the sweep/cleanup requirement) scored a clean 1.0 across all five facts — the agent recovered and correctly reconciled both herring/reversal pairs (g1.r2.h1/rev1 and the more obliquely-seen g1.r2.h2/rev2) into the single correct ordering: plan first, sweep only after planning succeeds, write new files, then the sidecar.
